--- title: "Model Diagnostic" sidebar: start --- The BF class can compute model diagnostics for a given model. Lets consider the following model for a linear regression: $$ Y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\alpha + \beta X_i, \sigma) $$ $$ \alpha \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1) $$ $$ \beta \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1) $$ $$ \sigma \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 50) $$ ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from BayesForge import bf import jax.numpy as jnp # setup platform------------------------------------------------ m = bf(platform="cpu") # import data ------------------------------------------------ data_path = m.load.howell1(only_path=True) m.data(data_path, sep=";") m.df = m.df[m.df.age > 18] m.scale(data=["weight"]) # define model ------------------------------------------------ def model(weight, height): a = m.dist.normal(178, 20, name="a") b = m.dist.log_normal(0, 1, name="b") s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name="s") m.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs=height, shape=(weight.shape[0],)) # Run sampler ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model, num_samples=500, num_chains=4) m.summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` /home/sosa/.local/lib/python3.13/site-packages/tqdm/auto.py:21: TqdmWarning: IProgress not found. R ```r m$diag$plot_ess() ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.plot_ess() ``` ::: ## HMC diagnostics: divergences and energy Check this plot first: if the sampler failed, the other diagnostics are not meaningful. - **Top row, one panel per chain:** the distribution of the energy E around its mean (blue, *marginal energy*) and of its change between two successive iterations, ΔE (orange, *energy transition*). When the two histograms have about the same width, the sampler can cross the whole posterior from one iteration to the next. When ΔE is much narrower than E, it explores the tails badly (typical of a hierarchical "funnel"). The panel title gives E-BFMI = Σ ΔE² / Σ (E − Ē)²; values below 0.3 are flagged with ⚠. - **Bottom row:** the number of divergent transitions per chain (ideal: 0). A divergence means that the integrator failed in a region of strong curvature, which is then under-explored. With a few divergences, raise `target_accept` (0.95–0.99); with many, reparametrise (for example a non-centred random effect). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.divergence_energy() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$divergence_energy() ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.divergence_energy() ``` ::: ## Posterior predictive checks All posterior predictive checks compare the observed outcome with *predictions*: datasets of the outcome simulated by the fitted model, one per posterior draw (`m.diag.get_yrep()`). Both are taken from the fitted model automatically, and the plots are labelled with the name of the observed site (here `height`, from `obs=height`). With several observed sites, each function returns one figure per site; pass `site=` to choose one. The idea is always the same: if the model is good, the data it simulates should look like the real data. For count or categorical outcomes, `m.diag.ppc_bars()` and `m.diag.ppc_rootogram()` instead compare observed counts with predicted counts per category. ### Density overlay Overlays the density of the observed data (black) with the densities of n predicted datasets (blue). The black curve should look like one more blue curve; a different shape (two modes, skewness, mass below 0 for a positive outcome) points to a missing group or a wrong likelihood. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.ppc_density() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$ppc_density() ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.ppc_density() ``` ::: ### Histogram small multiples The histogram of the observed data (first panel, black) next to the histograms of n predicted datasets ("Prediction 1", "Prediction 2", ...). The observed histogram should not stand out among the predictions; look at the number of modes, the skewness, the range and the number of zeros. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.ppc_hist() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$ppc_hist() ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.ppc_hist() ``` ::: ### Boxplots The box of the observed data (left, black) next to the boxes of n predicted datasets ("pred 1", "pred 2", ...): median, quartiles, whiskers and extreme points. The observed box should look like the others; an observed box that is systematically higher, wider or narrower, or extreme values that the predictions never produce (tails too light: try a Student-t likelihood), signal misfit. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.ppc_boxplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$ppc_boxplot() ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.ppc_boxplot() ``` ::: ### Test statistic Each predicted dataset is summarised by one number T (the curve is the distribution of T over the predictions) and T of the observed data is marked by the vertical line. The title gives the Bayesian p-value P(T(predicted) ≥ T(observed)) and its two-sided version: around 0.5 is fine, a two-sided value below 0.05 means the model does not reproduce this aspect of the data. Choose the statistic with `stat=`: `"mean"` (default), `"median"`, `"sd"`, `"var"`, `"min"`, `"max"`, `"q25"`, `"q75"`, `"skew"`, `"n_zero"`, `"n_pos"`, or (Python) any function of a 1D array, for example `stat=lambda v: np.percentile(v, 90)`. The mean is almost always reproduced because the model has a parameter for it; statistics the model does not fit directly (`"sd"` for over-dispersion, `"max"`/`"min"` for the tails, `"skew"`, `"n_zero"` for counts) are more informative. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.ppc_stat(stat="sd") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$ppc_stat(stat = "sd") ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.ppc_stat(stat = "sd") ``` ::: ### Predictive intervals One vertical bar per observation: the thin line is the 90% predictive interval (`prob_outer`), the thick line the 50% interval (`prob`), the white point the median prediction and the black point the observed value. About 50% of the black points should fall on the thick bars and 90% on the thin ones. Many points outside mean the model is over-confident; all points close to the median mean it is too cautious. Pass `x=` (a predictor) to see *where* the model misses. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.ppc_intervals() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$ppc_intervals() ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.ppc_intervals() ``` ::: ### Predictive ribbon The same intervals drawn as continuous ribbons (light: 90%, dark: 50%; line: median prediction) with the observed values as points. Easier to read than the bars when `x` is a continuous variable, here the predictor `weight`: the ribbon should follow the cloud of points over the whole range of x, without a curvature it misses. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.ppc_ribbon(x=m.df.weight) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$ppc_ribbon(x = m$df$weight) ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.ppc_ribbon(x = m.df.weight) ``` ::: ### Observed versus mean prediction Observed value (y axis) against the mean prediction of each observation (x axis); the dashed diagonal is a perfect prediction. A cloud of constant width around the diagonal is good. A funnel (spread growing with the prediction) indicates heteroscedasticity, a curve an unmodelled non-linearity, and a slope below 1 shrinkage (expected in hierarchical models, suspicious when strong). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.ppc_error_scatter() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$ppc_error_scatter() ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.ppc_error_scatter() ``` ::: ### Residuals Histogram of the residuals r_i = observed_i − mean prediction_i. It should be centred on 0 and roughly symmetric; a shift is a systematic bias, skewness a wrong likelihood family, two modes a missing group, and long tails a few badly predicted observations (see [LOO influence](#loo-influence)). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.ppc_error_hist() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$ppc_error_hist() ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.ppc_error_hist() ``` ::: ### Observed versus individual predictions Each panel plots the observed data against **one** predicted dataset (not the mean), so the observation noise is included and the cloud is wider than in the plot above. The width of the cloud around the diagonal should be similar from one panel to the next; observed values that systematically overshoot on one side mean the simulated noise is mis-calibrated. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.ppc_scatter() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$ppc_scatter() ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.ppc_scatter() ``` ::: ### LOO-PIT uniformity check For each observation, the PIT (probability integral transform) is the quantile of its predictive distribution at which the observed value falls: PIT_i = P(prediction_i ≤ y_i). If the model is calibrated these values are uniform between 0 and 1, so their density (blue) is flat around the dashed line at 1. The grey curves are densities of the same number of truly uniform values: they show how far from flat a perfectly calibrated model can be by chance, so a blue curve that stays inside the grey band is fine. | Shape of the blue curve | Diagnosis | |---|---| | flat, inside the grey band | calibrated | | U-shaped (high at 0 and 1) | predictions too narrow: the model is over-confident | | bell-shaped (peak at 0.5) | predictions too wide: the model is too cautious | | tilted to one side | bias: the model over- or under-predicts | **PIT versus LOO-PIT.** The plain PIT scores each observation with draws from a posterior that was fitted *to that same observation*, so the predictions are pulled towards it and the PIT values towards 0.5: a model that is over-confident can look calibrated. The LOO-PIT uses the leave-one-out predictive distribution instead, each observation being scored by a posterior fitted without it. Refitting n times is not needed: Pareto-smoothed importance sampling reweights the draws with the pointwise log-likelihood. `m.diag.ppc_loo_pit()` computes that log-likelihood from the fitted model automatically. When you pass your own predictions with `yrep=`, also pass `log_likelihood=` with the pointwise log-likelihood of the same draws, shape (draws, observations); without it the plain PIT is plotted and a warning is raised. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.ppc_loo_pit() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$ppc_loo_pit() ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.ppc_loo_pit() ``` ::: ### Predictive intervals sorted by observed value The predictive intervals with the observations ordered by their observed value, so the black points rise from left to right. The medians should follow the black points. A little "regression towards the mean" is normal (the smallest values slightly over-predicted, the largest slightly under-predicted, because the posterior shrinks them); a strong and systematic gap means the model flattens the extremes, for example because a predictor or a variance term is missing. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ##
